Life In The World Of Belavadös
A living atlas of weather, gods, peoples, ichor, transit, work, death, monsters, festivals, and ordinary survival beneath two moons
The painted face of Belavadös: drowned shelves, reef-bright coasts, green continents, island chains, and high storm mountains.

This guide is written for anyone arriving in Belavadös with a need to understand the place before it misunderstands them. It treats the world as a living society: roads obey rain, ports obey moon-pull, class identity carries public reputation, monsters reshape markets before they threaten bodies, and ordinary people survive by reading sky, rot, transit, and law together.

Belavadös is warm, wet, crowded, divine, rotten, engineered, and hungry. It has no white polar crowns; the far ends of the world are living coast, dark water, wet cliff, fog reef, rain-polished stone, and long forest. Ice exists where sun and ordinary weather cannot command it: in abyssal ice-crowns, pressure shelves, cold brine vaults, mountain remnants, brief harbor skim, and wandering omenbergs that frighten ships far from any cold horizon.

The world is not passive scenery. Weather has memory. Roads obey rain. Ports obey moon-pull. Factions obey transit. Class identity is a job, a social reputation, and a survival method. Monsters are not only combats; they are map terms, warning stories, food-chain pressure, disease vectors, divine traces, and reasons why settlement borders bend.

Every settlement lives by at least three clocks: the sun-year, the silver moon, and the copper moonlet. In industrial regions, a fourth clock joins them: the ichor inspection ledger. A person living in Belavadös learns to ask not only whether a road is open, but which moon is pulling, whether the skyship has cooled, whether the bridge fungus has been scraped, whether the temple bells have rung, and whether the nearest prison-god has been fed recently enough to remain weak.

The phrase most strangers learn first is not a blessing. It is a warning: The Hungry Gods Await. It means the divine powers of the world are real, imprisoned, exploited, and still starving. It means civilization survived the Gods by turning them into infrastructure. It means the greatest achievements of the age are also the greatest evidence of its moral failure.

2. Sky, Time, Moons, and the Star-River

Belavadös orbits within a relatively flat shared plane called the Celestial Road. Its year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days. Civil calendars keep eleven named months of thirty dates, while skykeepers, tide-priests, navigators, and observatory clerks track the small drift with temple clocks and harbor ledgers. Traveller-facing schedules may keep ordinary travel dates, but in-world record keepers translate them into Belavadös dates, moon phases, tide warnings, and sky omens.

blocks.text: The bright band crossing the night sky is the Star-River of Belavadös. In a world without modern skyglow, it is not a faint haze but a major geography of darkness, silver, dust, and rivering light. Farmers use it to time planting songs. Sailors use it as a sky-road. Funeral registrars use it as proof that the dead still pass beneath witnesses. Children learn that a promise made under a named constellation is never private.

Chandratecu-Seleneš is the great silver-white moon, broad enough to dominate public calendars and tide stairs. Mictlindra-Nannara is the smaller copper-gray moonlet that remains near the silver moon and races through a quicker cycle. Together they create layered tides: the large moon makes the public rhythm, while the copper moonlet adds fast pulses that can turn ordinary water into a sudden law of survival.

blocks.text: Constellation holidays are not isolated feasts. They are civic instruments. Bastveig's Tidehook closes reef gates for pilgrim tides. Ishtanora's Hearthdrum opens village storehouses and harvest kitchens. Enkirael's Warfire legalizes certain contests of arms while making unsanctioned duels easier to prosecute. Nephthysra's Mirror turns reconciliation into public art, while Freyseth's Mask blesses disguises, confessions, and threshold bargains. Nefarokir's month is feared because funeral ledgers, death debts, and resurrection petitions are audited together.

The most dangerous coastal days are not simply storm days. Danger rises when wind, pressure, rain, and moon-pull stack together. A modest storm can flood a harbor on a Copper-Silver King Tide; a powerful storm can spare a road on a Hushed Neap.
3. The Imprisoned Gods and the Pantheon

The Gods of Belavadös are ancient creators, predators, patrons, and prisoners. They shaped mortal peoples from design, hunger, curiosity, beauty, war, utility, and dominion. Their open reign ended only a few generations ago. The prisons that hold them are not merciful tombs; they are feeding engines, suppression systems, and extraction chambers built by rulers who chose control over liberation.

Ichor made the decision corrupt. Divine blood could heal disease, strengthen magic, extend life, fuel engines, empower curses, alter minds, preserve food, ignite industry, mutate bodies, and enrich elites. Destroying the Gods would have freed the world from divine predation, but it would also have collapsed the economies and miracles that depended on them. The ruling powers chose to keep the Gods alive, hungry, weakened, and harvestable.

This is why faith in Belavadös is complicated. A shrine may protect a village, a temple hospital may save a child, a god-mark may explain ancestry, and an ichor-fed train may bring medicine through a flood. None of that makes the Gods benevolent. The world lives in the aftermath of a victory that immediately became an industry.

blocks.text: 4. Peoples, Bloodlines, Alignment, and Social Reading

Every people in Belavadös carries a creator-god tradition. That inheritance is not destiny, but it matters. It shapes myths, prejudice, ritual custom, common occupations, marriage law, adoption law, military expectation, divine backlash, and the way strangers read a face at a border office. Mixed heritage is common enough to have legal frameworks, but rare combinations still attract temple attention, faction recruitment, and street superstition.

Belavadös does not compress morality into a single label. It uses four independent axes from 0 to 3000, with 1500 as the true neutral center and normal movement in 250-point steps. A person can be lawful but exploitative, cooperative but pragmatic, honorable while rejecting authority, or generous while chaotic.

The phase bands matter in play: 0-999 is extreme negative, 1000-1499 is skewed negative, 1500 is true neutral, 1501-1999 is skewed positive, and 2000-3000 is extreme positive. Alignment records in Belavadös are used by courts, temples, guilds, faction recruiters, and some magical ledgers, but they are descriptive rather than absolute. A person can change through acts, pressure, corruption, grief, divine exposure, and chosen community.

Humans and mixed-heritage peoples are treated as bridge cultures, valuable in diplomacy and suspicious when courts demand purity. Elven peoples carry moonlit, forest, wilderness, and hunter associations. Dwarven and gnomish kin are bound to craft, invention, stone law, and underground halls. Smallfolk cultures often control hearth trade, grain roads, inn law, and humble but crucial rural diplomacy. Orcs, goblinoids, giantkin, and draconic peoples are too often flattened into stereotypes by frightened cities; in Belavadös they possess their own law, poetry, engineering, food culture, kinship, and moral arguments.

Planar, undead, fey, elemental, psionic, construct, avian, beastfolk, aquatic, aberrant, plant, shadow, experimental, primal, and rare peoples are all part of everyday civilization. A rail station may include a warforged signal officer, a merfolk tide advocate, a goblin cook, a triton customs inspector, a tabaxi courier, a mycelian physician, a changeling actor, a dragonborn magistrate, and a dhampir death registrar without requiring the scene to become exotic. The world is strange; its bureaucracy is stranger.

Mixed heritage is handled through parentage, cultural upbringing, and creator-god resonance. Not every mixed person expresses every physical trait. Some inherit a visible body mark, some inherit social standing, some inherit resistance or vulnerability, and some inherit only the burden of being read incorrectly by everyone else. The most respected communities keep mixed-heritage registrars who understand adoption, chosen family, donor lineage, divine ancestry, and magical transition.
5. Disciplines, Multiclass Lives, Adventuring, and Quiet Work

Disciplines in Belavadös are not merely practical roles. They are professions, reputations, guild categories, temple expectations, school traditions, and public risks. A wizard may be a professor or a battlefield accountant. A rogue may be a criminal, a lock inspector, a salvage diver, or a perfectly licensed legal specialist. A barbarian may be a ritual warrior whose rage is a sacred weather-state rather than a lack of discipline.

blocks.text: Multi-discipline training as a life path

Multiclassing is common among mature adventurers because Belavadös demands hybrid competence. A storm cleric who learned wizardry can read weather as math and prayer. A rogue with ranger training can move through legal paperwork and marshland with equal ease. A fighter who becomes an artificer may understand both battlefield cost and machine maintenance. A druid-paladin may defend a river with law, oath, and root systems together.

Quiet life still contains class identity. A retired fighter runs bridge drills for children. A bard keeps market contracts audible and memorable. A monk teaches breath exercises to pressure divers. A warlock runs a threshold shop where no bargain is spoken without witnesses. Adventuring is not the only destiny of power; it is the loudest one.

Adventurers are tolerated because they go where institutions cannot act quickly. They cross closed tide roads, negotiate with monster-sign communities, recover records from drowned halls, escort ichor inspectors through angry towns, enter ruins before official survey teams, and take blame when a court wants plausible deniability. In return they receive money, favors, relic shares, transit priority, healing vouchers, faction attention, and enemies with excellent memories.
6. Ichor, Thundercoil Craft, and Divine Industry

Ichor is divine bioelectrochemical fluid: living residue, electrolyte, sacred contaminant, fuel, medicine, narcotic, mutagen, battery, and political leverage. The safest systems separate, dilute, bond, cool, ground, measure, and meter it. The most dangerous disasters occur when opposing fractions touch directly, membranes tear, catalysts overheat, prayer resonance overloads, or the living divine residue begins behaving as if it wants something.

blocks.text: The engineering sentence every apprentice learns is: Ichor is not lightning in a bottle; it is divine hunger forced into an electrochemical bookkeeping system. That sentence is painted above workshops because it warns against both superstition and arrogance.

Thundercoil devices translate charged ichor into controlled cyan arcs, contact discharge, pressure bursts, and overload effects. They appear as hand weapons, bows, rifles, shotguns, grenades, coil arrays, axes, hammers, swords, daggers, and ship-scale systems. Their cultural role is larger than combat: they are symbols of industrial modernity, class fear, worker danger, military escalation, and the public argument over whether divine suffering should power ordinary tools.
Handheld Thundercoils are regulated by charge capacity, maintenance seals, permit class, and visible cyan readiness glow.
Quiet coil-bows and scouting weapons are favored by rangers, skyship lookouts, and covert marsh patrols.
Coil arrays are area-denial platforms, training rigs, ship defenses, and desperate last-line machines.
Every overload has a social aftermath: witnesses, repair ledgers, injury claims, faction questions, and temple arguments.
Illicit Thundercoil parts often contain impure ichor, false saintglass, stolen prison residue, or forged inspection marks.
7. Transit, Public Infrastructure, and Travel Law

Belavadös is not a world where travel is a blank line between scenes. Travel is public law, weather calculation, class contact, faction leverage, and divine technology. Passenger times are settlement-local. Each 15 degrees of longitude equals one public hour from Belavadös Meridian Time, and portal travel still produces local clock jumps even when the crossing itself is quick.

All public routes depend on inspection culture. Faster transit is never free. Ichor multiplies power density and shortens routes, but it adds cooling time, legal handling, membrane checks, grounding plates, prayers no engineer admits are necessary, and the risk that a delay becomes a faction opportunity.

blocks.text: A commuter in Belavadös checks the sky before the timetable. They leave home beneath a roof still wet from night condensation, pass a fungus-scraper clearing a bridge post, and read the station board for weather holds, tide delays, ichor inspections, and local-time conversions. The train bell may say the route is open, but the ferry gate may close at Copper-Silver King Tide, the skyship may need an extra grounding cycle, and a portal hall may suspend crossings if the destination lock hears an omen bell.

Transit creates social mixing. A monk shares a pressure lift with reef merchants. A warforged conductor argues with a human fare clerk about sleep rights. A triton passenger carries water in a legal bladder. A rogue legalist buys a licensed violence bond in the same building where a cleric stamps flood relief forms. The station is not scenery; it is the modern face of the world.

Stations, harbors, docks, locks, skyports, submarine halls, and portal chambers are where government becomes physical. They contain customs desks, prayer alcoves, cooling yards, public clocks, food stalls, warning boards, guild offices, faction watchers, medical benches, lost-child posts, corpse registrars, and rumor markets. A transit map is a political map disguised as convenience.

blocks.text: The deep cold of Belavadös is not a white lid over the world. It is a hidden under-architecture. The abyss holds blue-black ice-crowns, hydrate stone, cold brine lakes, mineral chimneys, sleeping eggs, pressure-slow microbes, and god-sealed vaults.

When trench walls crack or deep currents lift fragments, an omenberg can appear far from any place that feels cold enough to make ice. Such bergs can carry freshwater, poison, old bones, living spores, alchemical salts, or the sound of the pressure shelf that birthed them.

blocks.text: 9. Biomes, Food, Homes, Childhood, and Daily Life

Life in Belavadös is abundant, but abundance is not comfort. Warmth speeds roots, rot, insects, fever, harvest, mold, and hunger. Communities survive because they work with the weather rather than against it. The best buildings drain, breathe, shade, flex, lift, close, reopen, and accept that repair is not failure but civic rhythm.

blocks.text: Food culture is preservation culture. Salt fish, smoked roots, fermented grain, pickled reef vegetables, fungal breads, pressure-dried kelp, hard travel cheese, spice-sealed stews, and temple-stamped emergency cakes are common. The wealthy eat fresh fruit year-round because they can buy cooling charms and sealed transit; the poor eat what survives humidity.

Clothing is layered for wet heat, sudden storm, mud, insect pressure, and transit safety. Reef settlements favor quick-drying wraps and shell clasps. Caverns favor treated wool, leather, brass fasteners, and lamp-reflective trim. Cities mix formal silhouettes with practical ventilation. Travelers carry spare socks, waxed bags, salt packets, fever charms, and a written local-time conversion if they expect to cross longitude bands.

Housing is elevated, ventilated, limewashed, drained, and repairable. Roofs are steep where rain hits hard, flat only where they are inspected often. Marsh homes stand on raised walks. Reef homes use waterlocks. Cavern homes use condensation gutters. Treetop homes flex in wind. Rich houses may hide divine wards in beautiful plaster, but even poor homes keep a dry shelf for documents.

Children learn sky, tide, rot, and route safety as basic literacy. A child may learn the four alignment axes before formal grammar because courts, temples, and guilds use them. They learn which monster names are literal and which are warnings. They learn that the big moon is not alone, that bridges need scraping, that a pretty cyan leak is not a toy, and that a god can be both imprisoned and dangerous.

Death in Belavadös is active. The death god maintains a design, a sequence, and a ledger for every living creature. Every soul has an appointed moment written into reality. Whenever someone escapes that fate through luck, magic, prophecy, intervention, or coincidence, the design fractures. The god of death responds not as a passive judge but as a force that hunts correction.

Unconsciousness is not merely blood loss. Reaching the edge of death means the ledger has noticed the soul personally. Candles gutter, clocks stutter, rain may begin, mirrors may crack, animals may panic, and nearby witnesses may hear distant funeral bells. A failed death save is death tightening its grasp; a success is not triumph but theft.

Resurrection magic exists, but it is not a clean reset. It may save a beloved life while moving pressure elsewhere. It may attract ledger-auditors, corpse rumors, omen animals, dream summons, or divine correction. Temples record resurrections as public spiritual events because an escaped death can change more than one person's fate.
A natural recovery can still leave a soul marked by cold memories, grave dreams, or a new fear of mirrors.
A resurrection may require witnesses, debt payment, a vow, a journey, a returned name, or a bargain with a hostile ledger.
Undead are not all the same: some are curses, some are debts, some are grief, some are legal mistakes, and some are deliberate resistance.
Necromancy is judged by context: funeral preservation, battlefield abuse, ancestral consultation, corpse labor, and resurrection theft are not treated equally.
Death festivals are part mourning, part audit, part appeasement, and part defiance.

Funerals vary by biome. Reef funerals may release weighted lanterns into tide roads. Cavern funerals carve names into condensation stone. Farming villages bake memory bread and distribute it before rot can claim the grain. Treetop families hang bells where the wind can speak. Cities file death certificates with temple, court, and transit office because an unresolved death can close roads, inheritances, and magical permissions.

Belavadös treats monsters as ecological and social facts. A monster may be a citizen, a plague, a holy sign, a market hazard, a faction asset, a weather metaphor, a food-chain pressure, a criminal partner, a legal category, or a reason a road was never built straight. outside-rule creature material is used as a bestiary language, but each creature is translated into Belavadös weather, gods, transit, death, and ichor logic.

blocks.text: Deep ruins in Belavadös are not empty mazes waiting for heroes. They are failed infrastructure, buried temples, prison-adjacent service tunnels, drowned archives, collapsed rail works, fungal cities, abandoned noble laboratories, old monster lairs, refuge networks, and places where weather can no longer leave. A good ruin has supply logic, waste routes, air, water, silence, old maps, new occupants, and at least one faction that wants the truth delayed.

Undercities matter because warm wet worlds build downward as often as upward. Mountain provinces carry deep cavern settlement networks. Coastal cities hide old flood levels beneath new markets. Dead stations become smuggler roads. Tombs become fungus farms. Dwarves, drow, tieflings, shadow peoples, miners, pressure engineers, and all those who prefer stone to sky make underlayers into real neighborhoods rather than background darkness.

Wilderness travel uses free movement, negotiation, ruin crawls, guerrilla routes, survival pressure, political encounter, and monster ecology. A lost-world island may preserve older beasts. A canyon may use rope and pulley law. A rainforest ruin may be more alive than abandoned. A reef may be an open-air ruin that floods twice a day. Every path should ask: who maintains it, what season breaks it, what creature reads it better than people do, and which faction profits if travelers vanish?

blocks.text: 12. Factions, Law, Economy, and Quiet Living

Factions are living Belavadös powers: offices, cults, orders, syndicates, institutes, courts, machine-priesthoods, and public-service bodies. They attach themselves to routes, permits, settlement danger, province government, resident peoples, and access to ichor. A job becomes public when transit, rumor, paperwork, and witness culture make secrecy too expensive.

blocks.text: Some provinces recognize forms of registered violence, salvage rights, prize shares, cleanup bonds, target classes, collateral declarations, and witness fees. This does not make crime safe; it makes it bureaucratic. A rogue may need better paperwork than a paladin. A killing may be illegal in one district, taxable in another, and spiritually catastrophic in both.

Belavadös economies are based on food preservation, route maintenance, ichor licensing, repair labor, weather prediction, transit access, monster-response contracts, temple services, document drying, salvage law, and faction patronage. The most important workers are often not glamorous: bridge scrapers, roof menders, tide clerks, apothecaries, condenser cleaners, route translators, corpse registrars, signal operators, waterlock attendants, and public cooks.

Not everyone is an adventurer. Most lives are made of water collection, roof repair, family meals, transport fares, gossip, worship, work shifts, market bargaining, seasonal dread, and small pleasures. Quiet people know which fungus is edible, which clerk is kind, which road floods, which station clock lies, which faction recruiter smiles too much, and which constellation makes their grandmother whisper. The chronicle world feels large when ordinary people have reasons to live that are not simply waiting for heroes.

Belavadös festivals follow the overlap of month theme, constellation witness, tide state, agricultural need, faction interest, and local disaster memory. A holiday is never only decorative. It opens markets, closes roads, suspends debts, permits masks, launches pilgrimages, changes patrol levels, alters transport loads, and tells ordinary people what danger society has agreed to notice.

A complete guide for players and Dungeon Masters
By William Saville, also known as The Transgender T-Rex #TheTransgenderTRex

I built this system to make alignment feel alive instead of frozen. Belavadös treats morality as a profile instead of a label, so characters can grow, slide, fail, recover, and surprise the table in a way that still stays easy to read.

This guide is written for Dungeon Masters, veteran D&D; players who know the old alignment grid, and new players who need a clean way in. I keep the language direct, the rules visible, and the moving parts organized so the system can be learned without losing its depth.
Nothing here is meant to trap a character in a box. Your choices shape your path, and your path reshapes your destiny.
How I want you to use this guide

For DMs, the recommendation is to start with the core axes, then move into the phase rules, and finally the XP sections. These pages establish how to run the system consistently and fairly at the table. For veteran players, the conversion material translates the old two-axis model into the newer four-axis profile system, preserving familiar ideas while adding precision and reducing ambiguity around labels. For new players, the first half of the guide is sufficient to begin play—focus on the axes, review the examples, and understand the difference between fit awards and shift awards. The appendices function as reference material you can consult when needed during play.
What I built this system to do

The system is designed to measure selfishness, lawfulness, cooperation, and honor as separate and independent questions rather than collapsing them into a single alignment label. This allows a character to be lawful yet selfish, cooperative yet dishonorable, or honorable while actively rejecting institutions. The result is a clearer moral shape that is easier to understand and roleplay.

It also emphasizes long-term behavioral patterns over isolated actions. A single act of kindness does not elevate a character into sainthood, just as a single cruel decision does not erase a lifetime of decency. Instead, Belavadös tracks patterns, turning points, sacrifices, betrayals, and repeated behavior to build a more stable and meaningful moral profile.

blocks.text: What I built and why it is different

Belavadös treats morality as a living profile rather than a single alignment label. Instead of compressing ethical identity into a fixed nine-box system like traditional D&D alignment, it evaluates a character through four independent axes. Each axis measures a different moral or behavioral pressure, allowing for more nuance and less forced categorization.

rows: Does the character give or take?
Willingness to prioritize others vs self-interest
Does the character submit to structure or break away?
Relationship to rules, systems, and authority
Does the character build with others or work alone?
Does the character keep an internal code when unobserved?
Personal integrity and consistency of values

blocks.text: This separation is important because real characters rarely fit cleanly into a single moral box. A selfish mercenary is not the same as a dishonorable traitor. A lawful bureaucrat is not automatically cooperative. A cooperative rebel is not necessarily altruistic, and an honorable outlaw may still reject institutional authority entirely. By keeping these axes distinct, Belavadös preserves moral complexity instead of flattening it into broad labels.

The system is also designed to reflect change over time. Each axis can shift as a character grows, deteriorates, or reacts to events. This turns morality into a dynamic record rather than a static label—allowing the system to track a character’s moral biography as they develop, rather than assigning them a single permanent identity.
Every character in Belavadös is measured across four independent moral dimensions. Each axis runs from 0 to 3000 points, and 1500 is the neutral center.

rows: Selflessness, compassion, and sacrifice versus selfish ambition and exploitation
Obedience to structure, rules, and duty versus rebellion and personal freedom
Group harmony, loyalty, and teamwork versus independence and self-interest
Integrity, truth, principles, and restraint versus deceit and ruthless pragmatism

blocks.text: If you only remember one thing from this page, remember this: the axes are separate. A character can be high on one axis and low on another without contradiction. That is the heart of the system.
Alignment phases, position steps, and crossing boundaries

I divide every axis into three phases. The low phase, the neutral phase, and the high phase each contain four tracked | positions on the character sheet. That gives me a simple, readable way to show not only where a character stands, | but how far they have moved.
Here are your contents organized into clear tables:

Leaning negative but still flexible. NPC reactions are mixed
The true center. Stable, adaptable, and open to many paths
Leaning positive. Trusted by like-minded NPCs and seen as dependable
Fully committed to the positive end. Revered or hated for strong conviction

blocks.text: When a character reaches the edge of a phase, they step into the next phase at the correct corresponding position. A | change of 250 points moves the character one position. Larger changes can leap several positions at once when a | major event deserves it.

At character creation, or through birth, adoption, awakening, or transformation in game, I let players start in more than | one way. They may take a short scenario based alignment test, choose their alignment manually, or build from a | background, oath, faction, or backstory that clearly points in a direction.

The default starting point for every axis is 1500. That means a new character begins at the neutral center unless the | fiction says otherwise. A DM may shift starting scores by about 100 to 300 points for an ordinary background, and by | larger amounts when divine influence, faction indoctrination, or a very strong concept justifies it.

I use those modifiers to create distinct personalities without permanently locking anyone into a rigid moral box. The goal is to give the character a believable starting shape, then let play do the rest.
Your actions continuously shape your moral trajectory. I do not treat alignment as something a player gets stuck with forever. I treat it as something that evolves through play.

blocks.text: A character can begin in one place and end up somewhere very different after one meaningful betrayal, sacrifice, or turning point. That is not a bug in the system. That is the point of it.

In play, I usually think in patterns. One kind act matters, but a repeated pattern of sacrifice matters more. One cruel | choice matters, but a repeated habit of exploitation matters more. The score should reflect the true story of the | character, not a single scene taken in isolation.
Why alignment matters at the table
Belavadös is not just a label system. It is a living reputation system. When the table uses it well, the world can answer the characters in different ways depending on how they have actually behaved.

blocks.text: That means the system can influence trust, fear, admiration, hostility, political standing, access to sacred spaces, rare dialogue, faction invitations, and the kind of legacy people speak about after the session ends.
I want the world to react to the character in distinct ways, not just say they are good or evil. That is why I separate honor from lawfulness and cooperation from altruism.

Belavadös replaces the rigid old grid with four continuous behavioral axes. That makes it easier to model gradual | change, mixed motives, and morally complicated characters while still staying fully compatible with D&D; 5e roleplay, | factions, magic items, subclasses, divine systems, and reputation mechanics.

I use the same reward logic for both advancement modes. The difference is not what gets rewarded. The difference is | when the points are handed out. My rule of thumb is simple. If a choice is merely on brand, it gets a fit award. If it | genuinely changes the character's direction, it gets a shift award.

I also keep the table honest by tying rewards to visible narrative consequences, not to table noise or repetitive point | farming.
Adventuring XP is the granular version. I use it when the table likes seeing immediate progress and wants alignment to feel like part of the normal rhythm of play.

When a choice fits the current profile, I count that as a fit award. When the choice changes the profile in a way that matters later, I count that as a shift award. A single scene can earn both, but only when both parts are true.
Milestone XP is the chapter based version. I use it when the campaign is narrative heavy, the table is open ended, or the group wants less bookkeeping during a session.

When old 5e content references alignment, I translate it into thresholds instead of binary labels. That lets me keep the spirit of the item or effect while making the requirement fit the new system.

blocks.text: A clean DM rule and the veteran player conversion guide

I use alignment as a living reputation system, not a punishment system. I award points only when actions meaningfully | impact story, relationships, faction standing, moral consequences, or character identity. I avoid rewarding repetitive | behavior farming.
For veteran players, the old two axis model still helps as a memory aid. I just split the old idea into four questions so it becomes easier to read mixed characters.

A character that was simply neutral in the old model | can land in many different places here, because neutral in the old system often meant the label was not trying to | describe that axis very strongly.
New player quick start and DM guardrails
For new players, the easiest way to use this system is to play your character honestly, say why they are acting when the choice matters, and ask me which axis a decision touches if you are unsure.

blocks.text: If two players make the same choice for different reasons, the motive can matter. Keep the table consistent and explain the rule before the campaign starts.

My fairness rule is simple. If the table can explain the award in one sentence, the award is probably clear enough. If it takes five sentences, I log the moment and settle it at the end of the session.
I do not punish imperfect roleplay. I reward intention and consequence. The goal is to help players explore the system, not to turn the table into a test they can fail by accident.
Optional rules and a session tracker
These rules keep the system tight when the campaign needs more control. They are optional, but I use them often when I want cleaner pacing and less argument.

blocks.text: Belavadös is not about assigning permanent labels. It is about consequences, reputation, ideology, personal evolution, social perception, and moral complexity.
Characters are remembered not for what box they were placed in, but for the choices they made when it mattered most. That is the idea I wanted this system to preserve.

If you are a DM, I want this guide to be easy to run. If you are a veteran player, I want it to feel familiar but sharper. If you are new to the table, I want it to feel readable instead of intimidating. That is why I built the system the way I did.
I wrote this guide to be useful at the table. Keep it close, use the pieces you need, and let the characters earn the shape of who they become.

blocks.text: The Design of Death in Belavadös

In most Dungeons & Dragons campaigns, death is a temporary inconvenience disguised as tragedy. Characters fall unconscious, allies rush forward with Healing Word, a potion, or Spare the Dying, and the party continues onward. Even when someone truly dies, resurrection magic often transforms death into a logistical problem rather than a spiritual horror. In Belavadös, that changes completely. Death is no longer passive. It is no longer a simple mechanic sitting quietly behind the dice. Death is an active cosmic force. It hunts. It remembers. It corrects mistakes.

In this world, the god of death maintains a design, a sequence, and a ledger that governs every living creature. Every soul has an appointed moment of death written into reality itself. Whenever someone escapes that fate through luck, prophecy, magic, intervention, or coincidence, the design fractures. The god of death responds by pursuing the survivors until balance is restored. This transforms the tone of the campaign from heroic fantasy into supernatural dread. You should stop thinking about hit points as abstract combat resources and start thinking about survival as something fragile and temporary.

To make this concept work inside Dungeons & Dragons 5e, death saving throws become narrative events instead of silent dice rolls. Every failed death save should feel like death physically reaching toward your character. Every success should feel temporary and unnatural. Rather than quietly marking successes and failures on paper, I will describe the experience in vivid sensory detail. A failed death save might feel like icy water filling your lungs, invisible hands pulling your soul downward, distant funeral bells echoing through darkness, flickering visions of graves, or whispers from unseen entities. A successful death save will not feel triumphant. It will feel stolen. Your character survives something they were never supposed to survive.

The philosophy behind unconsciousness changes as well. In standard 5e, reaching zero hit points usually means a character is bleeding out. In this setting, reaching zero hit points means the god of death has noticed your character personally. The moment you drop to zero, reality begins bending around you. Candles extinguish. Clocks stop ticking. Animals panic. Mirrors crack. Rain begins suddenly. Small environmental omens reinforce that death is not simply waiting for three failed saves. Death is already in the room.

Death saving throws themselves represent your soul resisting the claim of the death god. A success represents your soul dragging itself back into your body. A failure represents death tightening its grasp. Rolling a natural 1 becomes terrifying because your character briefly crosses into the realm of the dead and returns with fragmented memories of it. Rolling a natural 20 is deeply unsettling rather than heroic. Instead of simply regaining 1 hit point, your character violently awakens with visions of future deaths, prophetic hallucinations, or impossible knowledge they were never meant to possess.

One of the most important themes of Belavadös is inevitability. Death cannot truly be defeated. It can only be delayed, redirected, or bargained with. There are only two known ways to escape the design for any meaningful amount of time. The first is murder. By intentionally killing another person, a character steals the remaining years from the victim’s destined lifespan. The second is temporary death followed by resurrection. A character who genuinely dies and is revived becomes difficult for the death god to track because their name briefly leaves the cosmic ledger before being rewritten.

The murder mechanic is intentionally mysterious. I will never reduce it to a visible countdown or numerical timer. Stolen years function more like metaphysical momentum. A murderer becomes harder for death to claim because another life has been substituted into the design. The victim effectively takes the killer’s place in the sequence. This creates horrifying moral tension throughout the campaign. Good aligned characters may be forced to confront the possibility that survival requires evil. Cowards may become killers. Noble characters may choose sacrifice instead of stealing innocent years. Some may rationalize murdering criminals, tyrants, or dying enemies. Others may spiral into paranoia and predation.

Mechanically, I may track this through something called borrowed years. Whenever a character intentionally kills an intelligent creature as part of a conscious attempt to escape death, I secretly determine how much protection was gained based on the victim’s remaining lifespan and importance within the design. During this protected period, death cannot directly target that character through supernatural accidents or unavoidable omens. However, the psychological burden grows heavier.

Characters carrying stolen years begin deteriorating emotionally and spiritually. They suffer recurring dreams from the victim’s perspective. They hear the dead person’s voice in crowded rooms. Their reflection occasionally resembles the victim. Animals react with fear or aggression around them. Clerics sense spiritual contamination. Resurrection magic cast upon them may behave unpredictably. This ensures that murder never becomes a clean optimization strategy. Extending life through violence leaves visible scars on the soul.

The second survival method, dying and being revived, preserves hope without removing fear. In this setting, resurrection magic does not defeat death. It only confuses the design temporarily. When a creature dies and returns to life, the death god loses track of the soul for a limited time because the soul crossed the boundary correctly before returning. This creates an important distinction between ordinary healing and true resurrection.

Healing magic does not protect against the design. Healing Word, Cure Wounds, and potions restore the body, but they do not erase the fact that the soul was marked for collection. Revivify, Raise Dead, Resurrection, and similar spells genuinely interrupt the cosmic sequence. Low level healing is no longer enough to escape consequences. Survival requires confronting death directly.

Revivify becomes especially significant because it resembles magical resuscitation. The character truly dies for a brief moment before returning. During that instant, they glimpse the realm of the death god. Every revived character returns changed. Perhaps their body temperature remains unnaturally cold forever. Perhaps mirrors stop reflecting them properly. Maybe food tastes like ash. Maybe they hear whispers whenever they are alone. Resurrection leaves permanent marks.

I may represent these through marks of return. Every resurrection leaves behind a supernatural alteration chosen to reinforce the horror and atmosphere of the setting. One character may lose the ability to sleep naturally. Another may bleed black instead of red. Another might attract ghosts. Another may permanently smell faintly of grave dirt after rainfall. These changes are not meant to heavily punish players mechanically. Their purpose is narrative dread and immersion.

Death itself behaves intelligently and creatively. The environment becomes hostile in subtle escalating ways. At first, accidents seem coincidental. A chandelier sways overhead. A horse panics unexpectedly. Oil spills across stone floors. A bridge creaks ominously. Over time, the pattern becomes undeniable. Reality itself is attempting to complete the design.

These sequences are never meant to feel unfair. The horror comes from inevitability and tension rather than arbitrary punishment. There will always be clues beforehand and opportunities to intervene. A tavern fire begins with smoke, nervous servants, and crackling beams long before collapse occurs. A wagon accident begins with frightened horses and damaged wheels. You will recognize danger approaching even if you cannot fully predict how events will unfold.

Environmental hazards are layered together deliberately. A leaking lantern alone is not frightening. A leaking lantern beside spilled alcohol near frightened horses during a thunderstorm while an exhausted blacksmith works nearby becomes terrifying. You should begin examining your surroundings constantly. Ordinary environments become sources of paranoia.

Combat changes dramatically under this system as well. Battles stop being isolated tactical encounters and instead become opportunities for death itself to interfere. A fighter reduced to zero hit points may suddenly notice the battlefield turning against them. Broken pillars collapse. Loose arrows ignite spilled oil. A dying enemy accidentally triggers a trap. The god of death manipulates probability itself.

Resurrection magic across the world carries a darker reputation. Priests no longer treat resurrection casually. Temples fear repeated revivals because they attract the attention of the death god. Clerics understand that every resurrection creates imbalance. Some faiths outlaw resurrection entirely except under extreme circumstances. Others demand terrible sacrifices in exchange.

Diamonds used for resurrection magic become symbolically important in this setting. They may be crystallized fragments of souls that resisted death long ago. Each resurrection literally burns spiritual essence to obscure a soul from the design temporarily. Material spell components stop feeling transactional and begin carrying thematic weight.

NPCs who escaped death become deeply unsettling figures throughout the campaign. You may encounter a man who murdered dozens to extend his lifespan yet still sees death approaching everywhere. You may meet an old queen resurrected six times whose body slowly decays despite remaining alive. You may discover assassins hired specifically to kill marked individuals before the design escalates into larger catastrophes.

Visions are another major roleplaying element. Characters marked by death occasionally receive prophetic glimpses of future fatalities. These visions are fragmented, symbolic, and incomplete. A character may see shattered stained glass, hear children screaming, and smell smoke days before a cathedral collapse. Another may glimpse blood floating in bathwater before a noble’s murder. These visions create tension because disaster is coming even when its meaning remains unclear.

The order of death also matters. After surviving a catastrophe, characters may realize the design is pursuing them in sequence. Each death changes who is next. Every resurrection, sacrifice, and murder reshapes the order. The party may begin obsessively tracking the sequence themselves. Entire sessions may revolve around preventing disasters before they occur.

This naturally encourages strong roleplay because every character reacts differently to mortality. One may become recklessly nihilistic. Another may become deeply religious. Another may pursue immortality through forbidden magic. Another may emotionally isolate themselves to avoid hurting others when death eventually arrives.
At the center of the campaign lies one question. What are people willing to do to survive?

That question becomes even more disturbing when innocent people become endangered by the design. If death cannot reach its target directly, collateral damage escalates. Buildings collapse. Ships sink. Fires spread through crowded districts. The party gradually realizes their continued survival threatens everyone around them.

This creates opportunities for moral horror. A character protected by stolen years may remain temporarily safe while everyone nearby suffers escalating danger. Communities may fear those who have been resurrected. Entire towns may exile marked individuals. Some groups may argue that one person should willingly die to stop the cycle.

Exhaustion and trauma may reinforce the emotional cost of cheating death. Repeated resurrections strain the spirit. Repeated survival leaves psychological scars. Characters may become sleepless, detached, paranoid, or emotionally numb from constantly standing at the edge of mortality.

Death omens appear more frequently around marked characters. Ravens gather nearby. Milk spoils instantly. Insects swarm unnaturally. Strangers avoid eye contact without understanding why. Divination magic becomes distorted in subtle ways.

The death god itself remains mostly unseen. The less directly understood it is, the more frightening it becomes. It is not a traditional villain giving speeches or issuing threats. It behaves more like a cosmic law with intelligence behind it. It does not hate mortals. It simply restores balance.

Occasionally, however, its agents may appear. Pale masked figures, grave wardens, psychopomps, or silent observers may arrive near disasters or resurrection sites. Sometimes they simply watch. Sometimes they warn against further resistance. Sometimes they quietly collect souls after tragedy strikes.

Death is also patient. If the party successfully avoids one attempt, the pressure may vanish temporarily. Life appears normal again. Tension fades. Weeks later, another elaborate chain of events begins unexpectedly. This unpredictability keeps the atmosphere from becoming repetitive.

The structure of the campaign supports investigation based storytelling beautifully. The party may uncover records of previous death cycles. Entire villages may have vanished centuries ago after someone cheated death repeatedly. Ancient kings may have massacred thousands to extend their reigns. Hidden cults may worship the death god by helping restore the proper order.

Even undead creatures fit naturally into this cosmology. Ghosts are souls that escaped collection improperly. Revenants are beings intentionally allowed to persist until an imbalance is corrected. Liches represent ultimate rebellion against the design. Vampires survive by stealing life essence because they permanently exist outside the natural cycle.

The atmosphere of the campaign constantly emphasizes fragility. I will describe unstable architecture, old ropes, cracked glass, slippery stones, flickering flames, rusted chains, and exhausted workers with deliberate detail. Ordinary objects become threatening because the environment itself can become part of the design.

At the same time, moments of humanity become even more important. Quiet campfire conversations matter because survival is uncertain. Friendships deepen because nobody expects longevity. Romance becomes tragic because every future feels fragile.

Survivor’s guilt becomes unavoidable for many characters. Anyone who escapes through murder or resurrection eventually questions whether they deserved to survive. Clerics may struggle with their faith after reviving companions repeatedly. Paladins may break their oaths. Rogues may rationalize atrocities. Even successful survival leaves emotional consequences.

Prophecy also becomes deeply unsettling. Seers and oracles are feared because they glimpse fragments of the design constantly. Some blind themselves to avoid seeing death everywhere they look. Others profit by selling incomplete warnings. False prophecies become especially dangerous because misunderstanding the design often accelerates disaster instead of preventing it.

During major death sequences, pacing changes dramatically. Narration slows. Positioning matters. Every sound and movement becomes important. A simple tavern scene can become terrifying once every object in the room suddenly feels dangerous.

Mechanically, I want to avoid overcomplicating the system. The power of Belavadös comes primarily from atmosphere, roleplay, and tension. Standard 5e mechanics already support much of this naturally. Only minor adjustments are necessary.

One possible adjustment is preventing failed death saves from resetting immediately through ordinary healing. In standard 5e, any healing clears failed saves completely. In Belavadös, failed saves may linger until a long rest because your soul was still touched by death. This makes repeated knockdowns increasingly dangerous.

I may also track a hidden pressure system for each character. Escaping fatal events, surviving prophecies, using resurrection magic, or stealing years increases the pressure surrounding that character. The higher it grows, the more aggressively reality attempts correction. You will never know the exact number, only the escalating consequences.

Most importantly, Belavadös depends on everyone embracing the tone together. Death is omnipresent, psychologically oppressive, and morally corrosive. Survival always carries a cost. Fear, tension, investigation, and character drama are central to the experience.
Every combat becomes meaningful. Every resurrection becomes emotionally significant. Every death save becomes terrifying.

By treating death as an intelligent cosmic force instead of a simple mechanical state, the campaign transforms into something uniquely haunting. The question eventually stops being whether your characters can survive. The real question becomes what survival is worth.
In the end, the true horror of this setting is not dying. The true horror is discovering what people become when death refuses to let them go.

How to Read a Faction Page
Each faction page is built for play: identity, patrons, ichor posture, transit doctrine, location network, hierarchy, DM use, quest hooks, faction moves, rewards, complications, and a pressure clock.
Use for armored technology control, relic seizures, rail convoy drama, and tense lawful patrons.
Protect Belavados from uncontrolled inventions, divine-prison breaches, unstable constructs, and black-market relic trafficking.
Their containment laws can become prejudice against created peoples, awakened machines, and souls housed in engineered bodies.

A disciplined, oath-bound order that believes civilization survives only when the most dangerous inventions are catalogued, sealed, licensed, or destroyed. They do not oppose progress; they oppose unsupervised progress. Their chapter-houses resemble brass barracks fused with libraries, foundries, reliquaries, and armored rail depots.
Geisamahi auditors and artificers; Dragonborn line-commanders; Panolima engine-sentinels; Kaluseban field archivists; Deorbasun shieldbearers. No human membership is used in this conversion.

Marduthor and Setrimir define the order’s craft discipline; Nebyrr gives them a legalist obsession with registries and chain of command; Valkhamesh appears in their dragon-blooded command rites; Nefarokir haunts every sealed weapon whose last owner died without proper record.

Diluted ichor is permitted in emergency medicine, locomotive stabilization, rune batteries, and anti-curse sealants. Pure ichor is contraband unless locked under Warden seal; recovered pure ichor is often the first cause of moral failure inside the order.

Rail is the backbone: armored archive-cars, prisoner-cars, and relic-cars. Skyships carry rapid-response knights between major transit districts. Steamships and submarines escort waterlogged relics. Caravans reach villages. Portal passes are issued only to bonded quartermasters and crisis envoys.

A militarized arcane dominion founded by once-celebrated defenders who returned from a border war convinced that mercy is merely delayed conquest. The Diadem preaches unity through obedience, security through fear, and salvation through surrender to “necessary rule.” Its courts are lit by black-glass lamps, oath brands, and whispering command mirrors.
Shadow-touched Kaluseban inquisitors; Gwynis mind-seers; Aburata pact-cavaliers; Dragonborn storm-duelists; Volsarii death-notaries pressed into imperial service.

Enkirael gives the conquest doctrine; Freyseth supplies forbidden pacts and temptation; Eirzunet cloaks the courts in shadow; Nebyrr provides lineage law; Raeshkul sharpens strategy and psychic interrogation.
The Diadem taxes diluted ichor as a public utility and hoards pure ichor for command rites, fear-glamour, oath enforcement, and life-extension ceremonies. Addiction is framed as “loyal refinement.”

The Diadem prefers rail occupations, black skyship landings at fortified outskirts, and steamship blockades. Portal passes are granted to crown envoys, elite duelists, and curse-warrants. Unauthorized portal use is treated as treason.

Diplomatic rail passes, embassy skyship berths, courier caravans, steamship treaty routes, and emergency portal passes. Every portal pass is logged twice: once by the Concordat and once by Nefarokir’s death-notaries.

blocks.text: ichor-mutated swarm culture and wetland brood network

A living network of brood-colonies born from contaminated wetlands, abandoned feeding chambers, failed alchemical farms, and pure-ichor dumping. The Myriad does not conquer by banners; it adapts, absorbs, mimics, overgrows, and turns enemy tactics into new bodies.
Dril’thar mutation-clades; Panolima elemental broodforms; Jaspey spore-priests; Thoryn-touched insectoid and ooze lineages; Tamhiogal reef-symbionts who have not all joined willingly.

Diluted ichor accelerates growth; pure ichor produces command-nodes, brood prophets, and catastrophic mutation. Black-market dumping into rivers is the most common Myriad origin story.

The Myriad uses waterways, marsh channels, ferries taken over from within, and infected cargo on steamships. Submarine routes are dangerous because broodforms can cling to hulls. Rail infestations travel in grain cars, medicine crates, and livestock wagons.

Aburata civic-commanders; Gwynis compliance telepaths; Geisamahi surveillance engineers; Dragonborn mask-captains; Panolima barrier troops; Volsarii recorders forced into population ledgers.

Nebyrr is twisted into administrative destiny; Raeshkul drives psychic logistics; Eirzunet hides resistance histories; Oskar’enlil rationalizes engineered citizens; Enkirael keeps the boot on the throat.

The Lattice sells diluted ichor as rationed medicine and fatigue control. Pure ichor is used for compliance masks, memory stitching, soldier alteration, and ration dependency. Addiction is bureaucratized into an appointment schedule.

Rail timetables are their favorite weapon. Skyships carry inspectors between occupied terminals. Steamships and ferries move ration crates. Submarines police underwater approaches. Portal passes are numbered, witnessed, and revoked for whole families when one member resists.

rows: Use Earth date/time first for sessions, job boards, schedules, rail departures, skyship berths, steamship timetables, caravans, ferries, and submarine manifests.

Use steamships for rivers, lakes, harbors, bays, reefs, and seas. They are water-only sister craft to skyships, without sails or flight.
Use submarines for underwater settlements, deep-water prisons, reef routes, and faction-controlled covert movement beneath major waterways.
